chapters.title: 3 Making decisions
chapters.summary: How management chooses which feasible proposals to pursue, using weighted criteria, decision trees, ranking formulas and checklists.

blocks.text: Given a set of proposals for which the feasibility has been assessed, management must now decide which proposals to pursue. What decision makers are looking for is the **best option available**.

Decisions are too often made on the basis of personal inclination and interest, for ‘political’ reasons (enhancing the power or prestige of an individual or group), or in the absence of full information about risks and outcomes. Since a bad decision is costly, this section looks at structured, scientifically based methods of decision making.
Learning outcomes

items: describe an appropriate model for deciding which proposal to pursue
explain why profitability must be calculated in the same way for proposals being compared
calculate expected monetary value (EMV) in a decision tree
explain how proposal-ranking formulas work
use a checklist or measured checklist
state the main limitation of these techniques
list questions a decision maker needs to ask before deciding

blocks.text: The goal of decision making is to move towards a desired state of affairs through a series of rational choices from one or more alternatives. **Problems** are the gap between ‘what is’ and ‘what ought to be’. **Opportunities** relate to a potentially better situation based on current expectations.
The basic framework for rational decision making has six steps (McShane and Von Glinow, 2004, p. 236):

items: Identify the problem or opportunity.
Choose the best (or most appropriate) decision style.
Develop alternative solutions.
Choose the best solution.
Implement the selected alternative.
Evaluate decision outcomes.

blocks.text: When evaluating and comparing proposals, the most appropriate decision style is to be **objective rather than subjective** and **quantitative rather than qualitative**. Just as an architect uses a standard unit (a millimetre, centimetre or metre) to measure a building, structured aids can be applied to compare proposals.
Bazerman (2006, p. 4) recommends using weighted criteria to reach the optimal decision:

items: Identify the criteria needed for the objectives to be accomplished.
Weight the criteria according to their varying importance.
Rate each alternative on each criterion. This is often the most difficult step: ‘How well will each alternative achieve each criterion?’
Multiply ratings by weights, add up the results for each alternative and choose the highest sum of weighted ratings.

blocks.title: Coherence
blocks.text: The degree of relationship of the different parts of a proposal to each other and to the objectives and needs of the organisation.

The principle of coherence is an aid to ‘comparing like with like’. If two competing proposals use different methods of calculating profitability, it is very difficult to make an informed decision about which is better.

blocks.q: Why should profitability be calculated in the same way for competing proposals?
options: It allows like to be compared with like, so an informed choice can be made
It guarantees the cheapest proposal wins
blocks.explain: Different calculation methods make proposals incomparable, so the decision cannot be properly informed.

blocks.text: A **decision tree** is a way of representing graphically the decision processes and their possible outcomes. Trees are particularly useful when choosing a route where there are uncertainties about the results.

Example: you are developing a software product and must decide whether to **buy in** a package as part of it or **develop** one yourself. You believe good sales are more likely if you develop your own package, although this costs more.

blocks.alt: Decision tree: buy package (-10k) or develop package (-20k), each leading to a chance node with good or poor sales and final values 90k, 40k, 80k and 30k
blocks.caption: Figure 9 A simple decision tree (values in thousands of pounds)

items: **Squares** are decision nodes (options); **circles** are chance nodes.
The main decision is on the left: buy (£10 000) or develop (£20 000), with the cost shown against each branch.
Each chance node shows probabilities, e.g. 40% probability of good sales of £100 000.
The final rectangle (leaf) gives the total value of that outcome, including costs on the way. The top leaf is £100 000 − £10 000 = £90 000.

blocks.q: In a decision tree, what do circles represent?
options: Chance nodes with probabilities of outcomes
blocks.explain: Squares are decision nodes, circles are chance nodes, rectangles are outcomes (leaves).

blocks.alt: EMV equals the sum from i equals 1 to n of Pi times Vi
blocks.caption: EMV = Σ Pi Vi

blocks.text: Vi is the value of outcome i; Pi its probability, expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1; n is the number of possible outcomes, and the probabilities sum to 1.
The probabilities are *subjective probabilities*, perhaps arrived at through forecasting techniques; outcome values may be estimated with the financial appraisal techniques seen earlier.
Construct a decision tree to choose from three possible products and calculate the EMV of each option. Costs are in £k; the value of a product is higher if high growth is obtained.

blocks.title: SAQ 11
blocks.prompt: For each product, work out the net value of each leaf (value minus cost) and then the EMV. Which product would you choose? Write your values and conclusion.
blocks.hint: Leaf value = outcome value − development cost. EMV = Σ probability × leaf value.
blocks.model: Net leaf values: A = 15 and 1; B = 10 and −2; C = 10 and 0 (note a value can be negative). EMV: A = 0.6×15 + 0.4×1 = £9.4k; B = 0.5×10 + 0.5×(−2) = £4k; C = 0.7×10 + 0.3×0 = £7k. Product A has the highest EMV, so choose A.
points: Leaf value is the outcome value minus the cost of the whole path
EMV of A is £9.4k, B is £4k and C is £7k
A values can be negative, as for B with low growth
Product A has the highest EMV and is the choice

blocks.alt: Decision tree for products A, B and C with EMVs 9.4k, 4k and 7k
blocks.caption: Figure S.2 Decision tree for three products

blocks.text: The values at each leaf are the net benefits of the whole path from decision to the end of the path. The EMVs are £9400, £4000 and £7000, so product A looks best, on these estimates.

pages.title: Trees with more than one decision

blocks.text: A tree can include further decision nodes. In Figure 10 the primary decision is between developing product A or B. Product A is the one from Figure 9, so there is still the subsidiary decision of whether to buy a package.

blocks.alt: Tree with primary choice of product A or B; product A leads to a second decision of buy or develop package
blocks.caption: Figure 10 A tree with more than one decision node

blocks.text: Tackle the **subsidiary decision first**. Buying had the higher EMV (60k), so cut out the other branch and remove that node. Product A is at best £60 000, so product B (61k) is the higher-valued choice. Remember the likely accuracy of the estimates; there may be non-monetary reasons to choose A.
In a tree with several subsidiary decisions you eliminate each node in turn until only the principal decision is left, each time taking the branch with the optimal value.

blocks.q: In Figure 10, which option should be chosen, using EMV alone?
blocks.explain: After resolving the subsidiary decision, product A is at best 60k, which is less than product B at 61k. The estimates are close, so accuracy matters.

blocks.title: Try it: weighted decision matrix
blocks.intro: Apply Bazerman’s four steps: list criteria, weight them, rate each alternative and let the weighted sums rank your options.

blocks.text: Proposal ranking formulas

An unsophisticated technique, suitable only when fairly low expenditure is being considered. The viability of different proposals is compared by ranking them in order of **payback time** or **rate of return**.
Proposal selection index
Proposals can be ranked using a selection index:

blocks.title: I = PT × PC × NPV
blocks.text: PT is a measure of each proposal’s anticipated technical success, PC a similar measure of anticipated commercial success, and NPV the anticipated net present value.
**Checklists** assess various aspects of a number of proposals (in the source, R&D proposals) and are then used to compare options. Each aspect is rated on a key:
**Measured checklists** are almost identical, but instead of a scale from ‘unacceptable’ to ‘most favourable’, the aspects are scored numerically.

All these techniques require estimates of the **cash flows** over the economic life of a project and of the **probabilities** of outcomes. They assume it is practicable to supply the information shown in Figure 11. That may patently not be the case when a proposal has not even reached the drawing board, and gathering it is usually costly.

Sometimes the only alternative is to accept the risks of hunches and incomplete information, and to keep some rejected options open until the front-runner is evaluated more fully. Another approach is **sensitivity analysis**: try different values for the main parameters and see how they affect the final decision.

pages.title: Information needed for a capital project

blocks.alt: Flow diagram of economic and financial factors feeding the economic appraisal of an investment project
blocks.caption: Figure 11 The information needs of a prospective capital project (de la Mare, 1982)

blocks.q: What is sensitivity analysis?
options: Asking stakeholders how they feel about a proposal
Trying out different values for key parameters to see how they affect the decision
Removing all risky options from the tree
blocks.explain: It shows how sensitive the result is to variations in the data, supporting more informed decisions.

blocks.text: The creation of a project from organisational plans through proposals to decisions is often protracted. Certain questions need to be asked, phrased in everyday, jargon-free language. The decision maker is the person or people responsible for authorising a proposal.

blocks.alt: Cycle of questions: where are you now, where would you like to get to, how could you get there, how will you know when you have arrived, will it be as nice as you thought, then OK go ahead
blocks.caption: Figure 12 Decision maker’s questions

blocks.text: A project is the means whereby an existing state of affairs is transformed into a desired one. Before it begins, both states must be specified; the difference defines what needs to be done. Even if both are the same, the organisation may need to act to stop the desired state deteriorating.
A gap alone is not sufficient stimulus: the organisation pays attention to those problems and opportunities that its **value system** suggests are important.

blocks.title: Reflect
blocks.prompt: Think of a decision you made recently (at work, study or at home). Using the questions in Figure 12, describe where you were, where you wanted to get to, and how you would know you had arrived.
blocks.model: A good answer names the current state and the desired state clearly, lists at least two ways to get there, states a measurable sign of arrival, and considers whether the result would be as good as expected.
points: State the current situation (where are you now)
State the desired situation (where would you like to get to)
Identify alternative routes (how could you get there)
Define a test of arrival (how will you know)
Consider whether the outcome will be as good as thought

items: Base decisions on solid evidence; avoid political expediency and personal inclination.
A proposal must show internal consistency: no part grossly out of scale with the others.
Decision trees, proposal-ranking formulas (low expenditure), selection indexes, checklists and measured checklists can all help.
All need cash-flow estimates for the project’s economic life, which may not be feasible at decision time.
Sometimes a decision must be based on incomplete information; then keep other options open.

blocks.q: Which is NOT one of the six steps of rational decision making?
options: Choose the option favoured by the most senior person
blocks.explain: The steps are: identify the problem, choose decision style, develop alternatives, choose best, implement, evaluate.

blocks.q: Using weighted criteria, which alternative is chosen?
options: The one with the highest sum of rating × weight
The one with the highest single rating
The one with the lowest cost
blocks.explain: Ratings are multiplied by criterion weights and summed; the highest sum wins.

blocks.q: Decision nodes in a decision tree are drawn as circles.
blocks.explain: Decision nodes are squares; chance nodes are circles.

blocks.q: A decision has two outcomes: £80k with probability 0.25 and £20k with probability 0.75. What is the EMV?
What is the main limitation of these decision techniques?
options: They require estimates of cash flows and probabilities that may not be available
They only work for software projects
blocks.explain: They need estimates over the economic life of the project, which can be costly or impossible early on.

blocks.q: Which are suitable approaches when information is incomplete? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: Keeping options open and testing parameter values help; ignoring uncertainty does not.

chapters.title: 4 Projects: the life cycle, the project manager and success
chapters.summary: Project life cycles, how success is judged, why projects need managing and what a project manager actually does.

pages.title: A project’s birthday and the life ahead

blocks.text: Once a feasibility study has been undertaken, presented to management and a programme of change or one or more projects authorised, we can identify the project’s ‘birthday’ and think about the life that lies ahead.
Learning outcomes

items: describe the basic and extended life cycles used to manage projects
describe the product life cycle and the variation in processes for different products
list the criteria and factors used to promote project success
list the main activities and tasks of a project manager

blocks.text: a unique venture with a beginning and an end

The bit in the middle is where most of the work is done. A project has a **life cycle**, by analogy with living things that are born, grow, live and end. The **birthday** is the formal approval of a project, often a contract between client and supplier. A fuller analogy includes **conception** and the gestation period before birth.
Different animals have different life cycles and, like projects, every living thing is unique in some sense.

There is much discussion about whether there is one ‘true’ life cycle model or many. Some writers include the feasibility study in the life cycle; others begin only once the proposal is accepted, or when the accountants define cost codes and a budget.

We use the point of **conception**, even though that gestation period can be cloudy. The practical starting point is often the birthday, since management normally approve after the feasibility study. You can think of the feasibility study as a mini-project in its own right.
Real life is always more chaotic than the models we apply to it. Models help us recognise different ways of moving from beginning to end, and the broad phases where activities change type.

Each activity uses a known procedure at a given level of formality, starting with inputs from preceding activities. On completion there may be outputs known as **deliverables** (because they are needed for other activities). The order in which activities are carried out is called a **life cycle**.

cards.back: The order in which activities are carried out; the overall process for a given project.
A set of interrelated activities needed to achieve a particular outcome or deliverable.
An output of an activity, needed for other activities.
A highly detailed life cycle description with numerous forms, models and checklists.

blocks.text: There is no single life cycle for all projects, although certain types associate with a particular one. Descriptions may be very general (suggesting what to do) or very detailed (prescribing what must be done). Many writers use four phases. Turner (1999) used the life cycle of a plant:
Weiss and Wysocki (1994) use five: define, plan, organise, execute and close.

The change from one phase to the next is not necessarily abrupt. When there is significant overlap in time between activities in different phases (for example planning continues while organising is under way and execution has begun), these activities exhibit **concurrency**.

Since change is inevitable, activities such as estimating, recruiting or assigning work may have to be done again. Overlapping phases is also called **fast tracking** (PMI, 2004): it lets the project finish in less time than a strict sequence.

blocks.q: What is fast tracking?
options: Overlapping phases so the project finishes in less time than a strict sequence
blocks.explain: Fast tracking is the overlapping of phases (concurrency).

pages.title: The basic and extended life cycles

blocks.alt: Staircase of phases: concept, definition, implementation, handover and closeout (basic life cycle), then operations and termination (extended life cycle); business case and project plan marked as deliverables
blocks.caption: Figure 13 The basic and extended project life cycles

blocks.text: The basic life cycle fits many projects. The extended life cycle (also the product life cycle) adds **operations** and **termination**. The business case is the first formal deliverable to be given a gate review.

pages.title: Basic life cycle: concept and definition

blocks.text: The generic phases of the basic life cycle (APM, 2006):

head: Phase
What happens
rows: The need, problem or opportunity is established. Proposals are prepared and tested for feasibility. Sufficient plans are made for a ‘go/no-go’ decision, often a business case owned by the sponsor. The decision ends the stage.

Plans and costs from the previous phase are refined into a plan the project manager can use. During iterative evaluation and optimisation of the preferred solution, scope, time, cost and quality objectives can be affected as requirements are elaborated.

pages.title: Basic life cycle: implementation and handover

head: Phase
What happens
rows: The project management plan is put into action; design of deliverables is finalised so each can be built. Key activities: communication with stakeholders, monitoring costs, controlling quality, identifying and managing changes. The busiest phase of almost every project.

Final deliverables are handed to the sponsor. Once formally accepted, responsibility and ownership shift from the project team to the sponsor or users. The project can then be reviewed so lessons may be learnt.

blocks.text: The extended life cycle (also known as a product life cycle) involves supporting and maintaining the deliverables so the project’s intended benefits are realised. It adds two phases (APM, 2006):

head: Phase
What happens
rows: The period during which the completed deliverable is used and maintained in service for its intended purpose.
The disposal of the project deliverables at the end of their life.

blocks.text: Projects related to special events, such as an annual conference or a sporting event, make use of the extended life cycle.

pages.title: Try it: sort the life cycle

blocks.title: Try it: put the phases in order
blocks.intro: Sort project phases and activities into the basic and extended life cycles and see where each fits.

blocks.text: Each deliverable, whether handed to the client or produced in an intermediate activity, has a life cycle. Deliverables tend to follow a **product life cycle**, broader than the basic project life cycle (Dawson, 2000):

head: Stage
Description
rows: The initial investigative work: idea, feasibility, definition and planning.
The work done to develop (and test) the product.
The implementation, use and maintenance of the product.
The final withdrawal and replacement of the product.

blocks.text: The four stages are not mutually exclusive. For example, a manufacturer who installs a new production line in phases will see operation and retirement overlap: reduced operation of the current line and pilot operation of the new one.

There is also huge variation because of the variety of deliverables. A new university building and software to support online learning may have similar life cycles in outline, but their actual processes have very little in common. Section 5 discusses different approaches in software development, which can be used to compare processes in other industries.

blocks.q: Which sequence is the product life cycle of a deliverable (Dawson)?
blocks.explain: The first option is the basic project life cycle; the last is Turner’s plant analogy.

blocks.text: **Reviews** assess or survey something. They give a chance to reflect on what you have just done. They test whether the objectives in the project plan were achieved and assess whether the benefits in the business case were realised. A single focal point improves their effectiveness and efficiency.

blocks.title: Gate review
blocks.text: A formal point in a life cycle where a decision is made whether to continue with the next phase of the project (APM, 2006).
Reflecting on experience is an important step in learning, as in Kolb’s learning cycle (1984):

items: concrete experiences, followed by
observation and reflection, leading to
formation of abstract concepts and generalisations, leading to
testing the implications of concepts for future action, which lead to new concrete experiences.

blocks.text: Many small, incremental improvements can turn into major ones over time: one thing done differently each day could lead to 365 improvements a year. Learning becomes erratic when goals are not clear.

pages.title: Taking stock of the business case

blocks.text: Reviewing the business case is a potential turning point. Different behaviour patterns and work experiences lead individuals to make different assumptions about what they see. Internal relationships between stakeholders can lead to misinterpretation of the document, causing confusion and frustration. Taking stock early is a chance to assess what might happen in the whole project.

blocks.title: Apply the learning cycle
blocks.prompt: Take a piece of work you recently completed (an assignment, a task at work). Walk through Kolb’s four steps: what happened, what you observed, what you concluded and what you will try next time.
blocks.model: A good answer describes a concrete experience, reflects on what went well or badly, draws a general lesson, and sets out one specific change to try next time, which begins the next cycle.
points: Describe the concrete experience
Reflect on and observe what happened
Form a general lesson or concept
Plan something specific to test next time

blocks.text: When making a case for a project, part of the work is choosing the life cycle. Organisations that have used projects for some time often have a life cycle for the kinds of project approved. The simplest classification is by **industry** (construction, mechanical engineering, software, banking, health care).

Projects can also be classified by **outcome**: a product or a service, or often both. For example, a UK NHS project let GPs make hospital appointments in real time (service); a new software application (product) was developed to achieve it.

Combining *means* and *ends* (the **how?** and **what?** questions) gives four classes of project, according to how much is known about what you are trying to achieve and how. Obeng (2003) uses a metaphor for each, which helps stakeholders engage:

head: Type
Description
Example
rows: Sure what and how; linear and sequential.
Housing construction by an established firm
Sure what, unsure how; concurrent, converging on deadlines.
Sure how, unsure what; checkpoints where clarification is sought.
Developing new products for the market
Unsure of both; proceed with care, one step at a time.
Doing something new for the first time, e.g. a quality improvement programme

blocks.q: A team knows how to do the work but is unsure what the market wants. Which Obeng class is it?
blocks.explain: Sure of how, not sure of what: ‘making a movie’, with checkpoints for clarification.

blocks.q: A first-ever process improvement programme where nobody is sure what or how is…
blocks.explain: Unsure of both what and how: proceed with care, one step at a time.

pages.title: 4.2 Success criteria and critical success factors

blocks.text: There has been a substantial amount of research into evaluating projects, partly because the media report project failures. Researchers have established factors that together indicate a high likelihood of success. It is complicated because **different stakeholders evaluate the same project differently**, and evaluations change over time (Fortune and White, 2006).

items: **Success criteria** relate to the *what?* question; a mixture of qualitative and quantitative measures.
**Critical success factors** relate to the *how?* question; found in the project and its environment (a change in any factor is readily linked to project risk).

blocks.text: Criteria can be identified in the case made for a project; once started, the manager must also consider factors that influence it.

In the broadest sense, success is the satisfaction of all stakeholders. In practice criteria are narrowed to be quantifiable: whether **time, cost and quality** constraints have been met. Criteria differ with size, complexity and uniqueness, so there is no single checklist. Turner (1999) and Wateridge (1998) cover a range from quantifiable to broad:

items: the facility is produced to specification, within budget and on time
the facility/project achieves its business purpose
the project team is happy during the project and with the outcome
users are happy during the project and with its outcome
the project is profitable for the contractors
the project satisfies the needs of stakeholders

blocks.text: Fortune and White (2006) reviewed research into critical success factors and related them to project attributes from a systems viewpoint (abridged):

head: Attribute
Critical success factors
rows: Clear realistic objectives; strong business case
Effective monitoring/control; planned close-down/review; acceptance of possible failure
Senior management support; competent project manager; detailed, current plan; realistic schedule; good leadership; right choice of methods/tools
Political stability; environmental influences; learning from past experience; organisational culture/structure
Adequate budget; well-allocated resources; training; proven technology; good suppliers/contractors
User/client/sponsor involvement; appreciation of different viewpoints; effective change management

blocks.text: Each factor affects projects in different ways. A business case might contain a **prioritised list of critical success factors** reflecting the context. For each, there may be a qualitative or quantitative measure to monitor. Any variation beyond a threshold can be read as placing the project at risk.

blocks.q: Success criteria relate to the ___ question; critical success factors to the ___ question.
blocks.explain: Criteria are about what is to be achieved; critical success factors are about how it is achieved.

items: **Specify** what is to be done. This is iterative: pilots, feasibility studies and changes all modify the specification.
**Scope** proposals early for effort, time, cost and effects; plan dependencies between tasks and between resources and tasks.
**Agree a contract** on what, by when and at what cost; informal between departments or formal and legal between organisations.
**Coordinate effort and communication** among all players: organise the team, liaise with clients, senior management and users.
**Control** the move from plan to reality, correcting the course in a controlled way as changes arise.

blocks.text: A disciplined approach is very important in achieving a project’s goals and objectives.

pages.title: 4.4 What does a project manager do?

blocks.text: Project management is quite different from line (‘system’) management. Projects are designed to change something, so the manager must cope with the risk inherent in change. People may come from other areas, or be contractors, subcontractors or employees of consortium firms.

cards.back: Collect information on what needs doing and how it is organised, cost and duration, and interdependencies of tasks, skills and resources. Results: a project plan and budget.
The manager often has little say in who works on the project. The skill lies in making a group a team: motivating, managing conflict and ensuring good communication.
The manager manages relationships with stakeholders (the team is a subset), using communication to negotiate with and influence them.

pages.title: More duties of the project manager

cards.back: The spokesperson for the project: liaises with senior management, clients, regulators and all contributors.
Tools for managing, controlling, estimating and reporting; for software, from hardware and operating systems to compilers, test harnesses and CASE tools.
Manage the work done and coordinate team members and organisational bodies to achieve objectives.
Few projects end as planned. Without formal change control the project can deteriorate into chaos; a change control board of stakeholders may approve or reject changes.

pages.title: Try it: be the project manager

blocks.title: Try it: project manager simulator
blocks.intro: Run a project with stakeholders who have different needs. Combine planning, team, communication and change control to bring it in successfully.

items: Projects rarely proceed smoothly through well-ordered phases, but life cycle models have value. Projects follow a basic or extended life cycle.
All projects involve at least some risk; setbacks may need extra time, cost or rework.
Phases are not always clear-cut: design overlaps development, development overlaps implementation.
Check which success factors are present: the more, the greater the likelihood of success.
The project manager’s tasks: estimating and planning, assembling a team, putting tools in place, managing and coordinating work, managing change, reporting and liaising.

blocks.q: Which phases are added by the extended life cycle?
blocks.explain: The extended (product) life cycle adds operations and termination.

blocks.q: What is a gate review?
options: A formal decision point on whether to continue to the next phase
A review done only at the end of the project
A meeting with stakeholders about risk
blocks.explain: It is a formal point in a life cycle where a go/continue decision is made.

blocks.q: The project manager usually has complete free choice of who works on the project.
blocks.explain: Often the manager has little say; the pool is limited by skills and priorities.

blocks.q: In practice, project success criteria are narrowed down to which constraints?
blocks.explain: Success is assessed as whether time, cost and quality constraints have been met.

blocks.q: Which tasks are responsibilities of the project manager? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: Change management and reporting are core PM tasks; corporate strategy is not listed.

blocks.q: A change control board is a group of stakeholders who approve or reject changes.
blocks.explain: In more formal settings, that responsibility is given to such a board.

chapters.title: 5 Software development
chapters.summary: Why software projects are problematic and how waterfall, phased, prototyping and agile life cycles respond.

blocks.text: For many years, buying a software system meant almost all development was done from scratch: each act of development was unique or **bespoke**, like engineering in the early industrial revolution. Nowadays less software is developed this way. Applications come in boxes or downloads, known as **commercial, off-the-shelf software (COTS)**.
A **product line** is a set of related products sold by the same company. Software is also a major component of mass-produced items such as cars, televisions and mobile phones.
Learning outcomes

items: suggest why projects with software content are problematic, and how phased, prototype or agile approaches help
describe the elements of a basic software development process
describe the phased development life cycle and draw up a brief plan for one
describe the prototyping life cycle
explain why agile methods might be chosen over proprietary methods

pages.title: 5.1 Software is a different kind of product

blocks.text: Software is a rather **intangible** product, realised as texts of various sorts: design documents, program code, manuals, forms, and ultimately only in the observable actions of a computer system. Such systems may be highly complex and linked to many other systems, hardware and networks.

Intangibility and complexity make software prone to error. More size and complexity means more alternative pathways, so more chance something fails in use. A component not thoroughly tested (testing every possibility may take too long, or the circumstances may be impossible to simulate) will show its error only when it is too late.
**Malleability**, meaning software is easy to change, encourages changing rather than replacing it, on the assumption that this is cheaper. But every change introduces the possibility of new errors.

Errors in a program’s logic can often be traced back to errors in the **requirements**. Morris (1996) compared IT with other projects and found that IT is so intimately bound to its organisational context that issues of organisational effectiveness and user involvement are more complex and prominent, putting much greater emphasis on **project definition and user involvement**.

blocks.q: Why does malleability make software risky?
options: It is easy to change, which tempts changes that may introduce new errors
It cannot be changed after release
It is always more expensive to change than replace
blocks.explain: Every change introduces the possibility of new errors, though it feels cheap.

blocks.text: One factor in evaluation is the operational life of a product. A new building may be in use for more than a lifetime; a software product is rarely used beyond 10 years. So the choice of life cycle relates to the expected lifetime of the product: in broader terms, the choice of life cycle is **context-dependent**.

blocks.title: Why are software projects problematic?
blocks.prompt: In your own words, list at least four reasons why projects with a software content are problematic, drawing on section 5.1.
blocks.model: Software is intangible, so it is hard to show users and measure; it is highly complex, which makes it error-prone and hard to test fully; it is malleable, so changes are made lightly but each can introduce new errors; and many errors trace back to requirements, which are hard to define and depend on user involvement.
points: Intangible and hard to show or measure
Complex and cannot be fully tested
Malleable, and every change risks new errors
Errors often originate in requirements
Strongly tied to organisational context and users

blocks.text: Identifying a set of software engineering activities is the key to meeting the diversity of users’ needs. Each activity has a defined process, with inputs from preceding activities and outputs (deliverables). The sequence defines the overall development process.
A disciplined approach has three key elements:

items: **methods** describe the technical activities required to develop software
**tools** allow computer support for the methods
**procedures** are the glue holding methods and tools together, including project and quality management

blocks.text: Project management and quality assurance are part of the life cycle of every software project, whichever life cycle is used.
We assume the customer has assessed feasibility and decided a software system may be required. Methods normally include four activities (see Sommerville, 2004):

items: **Analysis**: identify the problem and decide what needs to be done; similar to defining a system and its boundary.
**Design**: determine how you will solve the problem.
**Implementation**: act upon the design decisions.
**Testing**: apply what you have done to determine whether you have solved the problem.

blocks.text: Some methods subdivide these or rename them (programming for implementation).
Breaking a problem into chunks means bringing the chunks together: **integration**, sometimes a separate activity. **Delivery** may be separate too, especially when payment is involved.
A system changes during its operational life. **Maintenance** allows it to evolve in order to:

items: correct errors
adapt the software to a changing environment
introduce enhancements required by the customer
improve the software in anticipation of future change

blocks.text: Analysis, design, implementation and testing are the backbone; project management and quality management are the glue. Maintenance itself involves all four and needs managing.
Arranging analysis, design, implementation, testing and maintenance in a single sequence gives the classic **waterfall model**. Even if each activity could be completed correctly, it has drawbacks:

items: A working version is not available until late in testing, assuming a patient customer and users unconcerned by the delay.
Errors found in the working version could be disastrous.
Real projects rarely follow a purely sequential life cycle.

blocks.q: What is a key drawback of the waterfall model?
options: A working version appears only late in the project
blocks.explain: The working system is only available late in the testing activity, delaying feedback.

blocks.text: An alternative life cycle **iterates** around one or more activities, keeping a core sequence. Iteration lets developers review outputs, and feedback allows the solution to be modified until it solves the problem correctly.

blocks.title: The tuning analogy
blocks.text: Tuning a guitar: pluck a string, adjust the tension, repeat. Tune another string and the first may need retuning. Only when all strings are individually and collectively tuned is the instrument tuned.

Partitioning a system into independent or semi-independent chunks called **increments**, developed sequentially or in parallel, is another way to form a life cycle. A small team might develop increments sequentially in a priority agreed with users. Where requirements cannot be split cleanly, extra activities manage dependencies and identify the interfaces between chunks.

Incremental development deals with complexity by **modularisation**, with tasks later putting the pieces back together (integration). **Timeboxing** sets a fixed period in which to achieve an objective, each box with its own deadline and budget (Stapleton, 1997). The team decides how to achieve the objective, and a deliverable may be modified to meet the deadline, with the customer’s agreement.

Whatever life cycle is chosen, it must reflect **what actually happens**, not a theoretical ideal. An idealised cycle is a fine starting point but must be modified; otherwise plans include activities that never happen and omit ones that do.
A **method** is an integrated set of techniques for carrying out the activities. It tells you:

items: the notation to be used and the rules for using it
the inputs and outputs (deliverables) of each activity
the process: how the activities combine to produce the result

blocks.text: The life cycle is the framework for the project plan; the method allows detailed planning of development and quality assurance. In practice methods seldom cover every activity; some cover only testing.

A good system must be fit for its purpose, and purposes vary: controlling level crossing gates, a chemical plant, an international stock market, a supermarket, a public library, a university, your personal finances, booking holidays. Users differ about what makes software useful, usable, reliable, flexible, available and affordable.
So there are different methods for different systems, and software companies often specialise (education, banking, manufacturing).

blocks.title: Example 9
blocks.text: UK government legislation often requires software for new administrative functions. Developers competing to supply it must conform to government-approved standards, such as **PRINCE** (PRojects IN Controlled Environments), which relates to project management and the quality of the developed software. They may also need an approved method for analysis and design.

This needs a formal process: slow and deliberate, but the result must deal with every nuance of the legislation and developers must show each aspect is incorporated. **Configuration management** controls the integrity of deliverables, ensuring they do not become corrupted or inconsistent.

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.text: In certain financial areas, being first to market with a new service gives the most profit. Development is almost a race: do the simplest things that could possibly work, minimise communication, use very few developers (say two) and a minimal set of agreed procedures. Less code means fewer bugs and fewer tests, but there must still be testing and some documentation.
The scope is narrow, so fewer changes are expected in the short development time.

blocks.q: Which example would suit a formal, well-documented process?
blocks.explain: Example 9 needs formality and evidence; Example 10 needs speed and minimal procedure.

items: **Size:** teams of up to eight can communicate and respond informally; larger projects need a well-defined procedure. Large groups split into smaller teams with specialists (analysts, designers, programmers).
**Lifetime:** include expected lifetime in risk assessment. In Example 10 lifetime is short, so a slow process is inappropriate.
**Risk:** iterate on the whole life cycle to manage risk. Missing the market window makes software worthless regardless of how much is built.

blocks.text: Major risks lie in the requirements: do you understand them all, and are they changing too often? Reviews help, as for each decision there is a risk it is wrong.

Desirable features usually exceed what a given price and timescale can deliver, so choices must be made. One approach is to estimate the **risk of not delivering each feature**: if it did not appear in the final product, what effect would that have on usability, usefulness, reliability and flexibility?

blocks.title: Prioritise features
blocks.prompt: You must deliver an online library-loans system within a fixed budget and cannot build everything. Explain how you would decide which features to include or drop.
blocks.model: Estimate the risk of not delivering each feature: ask what effect omitting it would have on usability, usefulness, reliability and flexibility. Keep the features whose absence carries the highest risk, agree priorities with users, and use timeboxes or increments so the most important features are delivered first.
points: Estimate the risk of not delivering each feature
Consider effect on usability, usefulness, reliability and flexibility
Agree priorities with users
Deliver the most important features first, e.g. in increments

blocks.text: **Phased development** repeats requirements determination, evaluation of alternatives, design specification and implementation over several iterations, forming a series of closely linked mini-projects (each may be large). At the end of each, some portion is implemented and reviewed by users, and the feedback helps determine the requirements of the next.

blocks.alt: Four phases side by side, each with determine requirements, evaluate alternatives, specify design, implement design, and user review; phase 4 ends with changeover
blocks.caption: Figure 14 A phased development life cycle (Jordan and Machesky, 1990)

blocks.text: A large insurer decided to automate claims handling **in phases** because:

items: earlier attempts to automate major functions had caused costly problems
few resources were available, so no concentrated single effort was possible
disruption to the claims adjustment department would be minimised
training could occur bit by bit, naturally
user feedback at each phase would inform the next

blocks.text: The phases mirrored the path of a claim through the department to adjudication and payment.

items: **Phase 1:** an on-screen claims form filled in by an operator on the telephone; soon entered directly via headsets. The form was printed and posted for checking and signature.
**Phase 2:** minor improvements; once approved by the claimant, the form went electronically to the adjuster, who entered repairers’ quotations; arithmetic was automatic.
**Phase 3:** minor improvements; approval by the adjuster and quality control by a manager were automated; cheques printed, plus a report of rejected claims.
**Phase 4:** word processing helped prepare letters to claimants whose claims were rejected or needed more information, with standard phrases plus custom paragraphs.

blocks.text: Phased development suits projects with a high degree of technological risk or where resources are not available to do everything in one effort. Benefits: minimal disruption and several points where feedback can change the end product.

blocks.title: Draw up a brief phased plan
blocks.prompt: A small college wants to replace its paper-based course enrolment with an online system. Outline a plan in three phases and say what users review at the end of each.
blocks.hint: Start with the most basic function, then build outwards, as the insurance example did.
blocks.model: Phase 1: online enrolment form for staff to enter student details, review by registry staff. Phase 2: students enrol themselves; automatic checks for course capacity and prerequisites; review with a pilot group of students. Phase 3: payments, confirmation emails and reports for tutors; final review and changeover. Each phase repeats requirements, alternatives, design and implementation, and the feedback informs the next phase.
points: Split the work into a small number of sequential phases
Start with the simplest, most valuable function
Each phase repeats requirements, design and implementation
End each phase with a user review
Use the feedback to set the next phase’s requirements

blocks.text: **Prototyping** is a form of phased development. A model, or prototype, of the proposed system is built quickly and shown to users to obtain rapid feedback. It may or may not become part of the final system.

It reserves the right to throw away a less successful model, build on a more successful one and fine-tune a very successful one. A prototype may begin crude (ignoring function to study, say, ergonomics) and be refined, be rebuilt at each iteration, or after several iterations a ‘formal’ project may turn the approved model into a working system.
Advantages are similar to phased development. The disadvantage: costs and schedules are far harder to estimate (early prototypes are experimental) and projects harder to control.

Proprietary processes demand particular documents to particular standards, with heavy record keeping. Engineers dislike being distracted from developing software, and managers dislike the cost. A manager does not want to lose control, nor alienate the engineers they depend upon.

**Agile methods** emerged in response. They draw on the informal approach of small teams, in the US sometimes called ‘skunk works’: a small team outside normal company policies, with a tight schedule and an ambitious project. Agile methods make explicit what such teams do tacitly, and make it acceptable to managers and stakeholders.
The Manifesto for Agile Development was drawn up in February 2001 by the Agile Alliance, using the concepts of increments, prototyping and timeboxing. For example:

Our highest priority is to satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software. Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale. Working software is the primary measure of progress.
Agile methods do not prescribe what should be done when; they recognise that what an engineer does depends on the situation. Teams reflect regularly on how to be more effective and adjust.

pages.title: Try it: pick the right method

blocks.title: Try it: which development process?
blocks.intro: Describe a project (size, risk, requirement stability, time pressure) and see whether waterfall, phased, prototyping or agile fits best, and why.

blocks.text: Real life is messy and projects run into problems. Life cycle models are still useful for planning, guiding stages and helping a manager, as long as it is remembered that the model is only a model, not an exact description. **More important than the life cycle are the milestones and deliverables agreed in the project plan.**

blocks.q: According to the text, what matters more than the chosen life cycle?
options: The milestones and deliverables agreed in the project plan
blocks.explain: The life cycle is a model; milestones and deliverables are what the plan commits to.

blocks.text: There are no widely agreed measures of the ‘goodness’ of software; quality measures are largely confined to the relative absence of faults. One study (adapted from Norris et al., 1993) looked at faults by phase:

Requirements definition comes first: an analyst interviews and observes clients and users. The product is intangible, so little can be shown to them. Users may not understand software capabilities and complexities, may struggle to express requirements, and analysts are rarely experts in the client’s business.

A walk-through of a requirements document makes it hard to tell whether all requirements are covered. One solution is a **prototype**, crudely giving the function and feel of the product, so deficiencies can be found and the definition refined.

pages.title: Faults from design, installation and operation

items: **Design** is plagued by change: with nothing tangible it seems anything can be changed simply, but complexity means knock-on effects are hard to see until testing. Prototyping and phased development help, though control problems and extra time can make them unsatisfactory.
**Installation** gives the fewest significant errors: relatively straightforward, though the team may not feel so.
**Operation** reveals many errors due to complexity; a fix in one area can cascade, so maintenance can be a project in its own right.

blocks.text: Software development involves a series of **translations**: requirements to design, design to a programming language, then to machine language. At each step something may be missed, inserted or mistranslated, and simple errors, like a full stop for a comma, can have enormous effects.

Even flawed software can be an enormous boon for daily tasks. If a word processor prints one page instead of a whole document, it is annoying but not threatening. The consequences are far more serious in software that flies aircraft, monitors airport radar, manages power stations or runs systems in motor cars.

blocks.q: Which phase gave rise to the largest share of faults in the study (Table 16)?
blocks.explain: Requirements definition accounted for 38% of faults.

blocks.text: Projects with significant software content are particularly problematic. Software can be treated as a product, though less tangible than furniture. It is difficult to measure, very complex and subject to human error as outputs of one phase are translated for the next, most seriously where it is critical to human safety.
Software development is similar to engineering when it involves a defined process with clear activities, each with one or more products that can be tested against the user’s requirements.

cards.back: Single sequence of analysis, design, implementation, testing and maintenance.
A series of mini-projects, each ending in user review that informs the next.
Quickly build a model to get rapid user feedback; may be thrown away or refined.
Light-documentation, frequent delivery of working software, regular team reflection.
A fixed period with its own deadline and budget to achieve an objective.

blocks.q: Which are the four core software development activities?
blocks.explain: These four are the backbone of software engineering practice.

blocks.q: Which is NOT a reason for maintenance?
blocks.explain: Maintenance corrects, adapts, enhances and improves in anticipation of change.

blocks.q: Prototypes are always thrown away once the real system is built.
blocks.explain: A prototype may or may not become part of the final system.

blocks.q: A project with high technological risk and limited resources suits which life cycle?
blocks.explain: Phased development suits high technological risk or limited resources, with minimal disruption and repeated feedback.

blocks.q: Why might agile methods be chosen over proprietary methods?
options: They avoid heavy documentation and bureaucracy while keeping delivery frequent
They remove the need for testing
blocks.explain: Agile methods reduce record-keeping overhead and focus on frequent working software.

blocks.q: Which are disadvantages of prototyping? Select all that apply.
options: Costs and schedules are hard to estimate
blocks.explain: Prototyping gives early user feedback, but is experimental and harder to estimate and control.

blocks.text: This free course provided an introduction to studying Management. It took you through a series of exercises designed to develop your approach to study and learning at a distance and helped to improve your confidence as an independent learner.
Key take-aways

items: A project is a unique venture with a beginning and an end; it moves from an existing to a desired state.
Decisions should be objective and quantitative: weighted criteria, decision trees and EMV, checklists, while remembering their dependence on estimates.
Projects follow a basic or extended life cycle; the milestones and deliverables matter more than the model.
Success is judged by criteria (what) and critical success factors (how).
The project manager plans, builds the team, manages stakeholders, coordinates work and controls change.
Software is intangible, complex and malleable; phased, prototype and agile approaches help manage that.
